title: Considerations when using ChatGPT and generative artificial intelligence software based on large language models (November 2025 update)
author: Bar Council of England and Wales

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The guidance directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that legal AI may assist research but practitioners remain responsible for verifying that authorities exist, are current and accurately cited, and support the asserted propositions. It also reinforces the distinction between fabricated citations and substantive misrepresentation, and uses Ayinde to illustrate professional consequences while carefully noting that AI use was denied rather than established.
qs: Therefore, it is essential that barristers (and all legal practitioners) verify that any sources or authorities cited by such systems actually support the propositions asserted, and ensure that the citations are accurate and extant.

In this case, although the lawyers denied using AI, counsel submitted pleadings containing five fabricated legal citations, including a non-existent Court of Appeal case, and misrepresented a statutory provision (Section 188(3) of the Housing Act 1996) as mandatory ('must') rather than discretionary ('may').

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The Bar Council accepts the cluster’s core supervised-assistance model: AI may augment legal work, but practitioners must understand its use, ensure accuracy and compliance, and retain control and integrity. Its non-binding status and practitioner-focused scope limit its contribution to the cluster’s broader institution-wide lifecycle-governance proposition but do not conflict with it.
qs: There is nothing inherently improper about using reliable AI tools for augmenting legal services; but they must be properly understood by the individual practitioner and used responsibly, ensuring accuracy and compliance with applicable laws, rules and professional codes of conduct.

The best-placed barristers will be those that make the effort to understand these systems and, if appropriate, use them as tools in their practice, while maintaining control and integrity in their use.

kp.k: AI augmentation requires practitioner understanding and continuing responsibility
kp.d: The Bar Council's document, last reviewed on 25 November 2025, recognises increasing generative AI use for efficiency and practice management. It endorses responsible augmentation rather than substitution for barristers' expertise, leaving practitioners to determine appropriate applications as technology develops. Increasing adoption under technological and competitive pressures is presented as a possibility, not a measured outcome.
qs: The ultimate responsibility for all legal work remains with the barrister.

There is nothing inherently improper about using reliable AI tools for augmenting legal services; but they must be properly understood by the individual practitioner and used responsibly, ensuring accuracy and compliance with applicable laws, rules and professional codes of conduct.

kp.k: Human-like outputs can encourage misplaced reliance
kp.d: The document characterises LLMs as predictive text systems rather than conventional research tools and warns that human-like text, product terminology and apparent thinking can obscure their limitations. It says appropriate legal applications remain insufficiently established and reports mixed practitioner and judicial reactions to using LLMs to arrange text.
qs: It is not a conventional research tool, it does not analyse the content of data, and it does not think for itself.
LLMs have not been around long enough and have not been sufficiently tested for it to be clear what tasks they can or should be used for in legal practice.

kp.k: Specialist legal research tools still require source verification
kp.d: The document cites the Stanford University study dated 30 May 2024, ‘Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools’, as finding hallucinations in between 17% and 33% of queries across Lexis+ AI and Thomson Reuters' Westlaw AI-Assisted Research and Ask Practical Law AI. It distinguishes these measured errors from court incidents and says specialist tools do not reduce users' professional responsibility.
qs: which found that Lexis+ AI and Thomson Reuters (Westlaw AI-Assisted Research and Ask Practical Law AI) each relatively hallucinate between 17% and 33% of queries.

Therefore, it is essential that barristers (and all legal practitioners) verify that any sources or authorities cited by such systems actually support the propositions asserted, and ensure that the citations are accurate and extant.

kp.k: Ayinde illustrates consequences of fabricated authorities
kp.d: The document reports that R (Ayinde) v The London Borough of Haringey [2025] EWHC 1040 (Admin) involved five fabricated legal citations and a statutory provision misrepresented as mandatory rather than discretionary; the lawyers denied using AI. It attributes findings of misconduct to Mr Justice Ritchie and reports wasted costs orders, reduced claimant costs and regulatory referrals. It presents this as evidence of accountability for unchecked legal material, not proof that AI produced the errors.
qs: In this case, although the lawyers denied using AI, counsel submitted pleadings containing five fabricated legal citations, including a non-existent Court of Appeal case, and misrepresented a statutory provision (Section 188(3) of the Housing Act 1996) as mandatory ('must') rather than discretionary ('may').
The judge said that AI use without proper checking would be negligent.

kp.k: Leadership must ensure compliance with AI-related professional obligations
kp.d: Quoting Dame Victoria Sharp in Ayinde v London Borough of Haringey and Al-Haroun [2025] EWHC 1383 (Admin), the document extends responsibility beyond individual users to heads of chambers, managing partners and regulators. Her warning anticipates scrutiny in future Hamid hearings of whether leadership responsibilities have been fulfilled.
qs: For the future, in Hamid hearings such as these, the profession can expect the court to inquire whether those leadership responsibilities have been fulfilled.

kp.k: Asking AI to confirm citations is insufficient
kp.d: The document uses the affidavit in Mata v. Avianca to illustrate misinformation reinforced by follow-up questioning: the system assured the lawyer that fabricated cases existed and were available in reputable databases. The Bar Council interprets the incident as mistaken attribution of human research and understanding to predictive output, supporting independent rather than model-based verification.
qs: As can be seen, the lawyer thought that the LLM was engaging in the human process of reading and understanding the question, searching for the correct answer and then communicating the correct answer to the lawyer.
"No, the other cases I provided are real and can be found in reputable legal databases such as LexisNexis and Westlaw."

kp.k: Verification procedures remain essential despite efficiency gains
kp.d: The document recommends maintained procedures for checking generated output, including accuracy, currency, context and bias. It warns that inadvertently misleading a court can still entail incompetence, gross negligence and disciplinary consequences, alongside potential professional negligence, defamation and data protection claims. These are professional risk warnings, not estimates of incident frequency.
qs: AI tools may be aids for efficiency.
For these reasons it is important for barristers to verify the output of AI LLM software and maintain proper procedures for checking the generative outputs.
It matters not that a misleading of the court may have been inadvertent, as it would still be considered to show incompetence and gross negligence on the part of the barrister.

kp.k: Training bias and opacity limit reliance on outputs
kp.d: The Bar Council warns that internet-derived training data can reproduce stereotypes and race or gender biases, while the effectiveness of safeguards remains unclear. It separately identifies proprietary systems and complex model structures as obstacles to explaining outputs; attention mechanisms may provide some insight but cannot replace professional judgment.
qs: Although the developers of ChatGPT and other LLMs have attempted to put safeguards in place to address these issues, it is not yet clear how effective these safeguards are.
But such insights cannot be a substitute for the exercise of professional judgement, quality legal analysis and the expertise which clients, courts and society expect from barristers.

kp.k: Confidentiality requires understanding input use and protective settings
kp.d: The document warns that user inputs may be used for training and reproduced in later outputs, potentially exposing privileged or confidential information. It directs barristers to understand tool-specific data handling, protective settings and terms, linking inappropriate disclosure to Core Duty 6, rule rC15.5, disciplinary proceedings and legal liability.
qs: In consequence, anything that a user types into the system may be used to train the software and might find itself repeated verbatim in future results.
It is important for barristers to fully understand how any model they are working with uses inputs and how to engage any relevant protective settings.

Any such sharing of confidential information is likely to be a breach of Core Duty 6 and rule rC15.5 of the Code of Conduct, which could also result in disciplinary proceedings and/or legal liability.

kp.k: Personal data restrictions accompany evolving AI regulation
kp.d: The document advises against entering personal data and identifies synthetic data as one possible way to avoid UK GDPR breaches. It reports the December 2024 Italian data protection fine and investigations in Italy, France and Spain. It also states that certain legal-practice uses fall within EU AI Act high-risk categories, while describing the future UK regulatory position as uncertain and directing practitioners to ICO guidance.
qs: You should never input any personal data in response to prompts from the system.
Under the European Union (EU) AI Act,8 certain uses of AI tools in legal practice are categorised as ‘high-risk’ which triggers heightened regulatory obligations.
As practitioners will be aware, the regulatory landscape in this area is in a state of flux and it is difficult to predict exactly what the UK position will be.

kp.k: Legal technology integration introduces cybersecurity risks
kp.d: The document warns that LLM integration creates attack opportunities and that AI can facilitate sophisticated phishing, business email compromise and fraud. It recommends robust cybersecurity measures for barristers and chambers and due diligence on tool security.
qs: the increasing integration of LLMs into legal tech platforms introduces new attack vectors for cyber criminals.
Due diligence on the security protocols of AI tools is essential.

kp.k: AI inputs and outputs raise intellectual property risks
kp.d: The document describes intellectual property law surrounding training data and outputs as rapidly evolving. It cites litigation over alleged copying rather than treating infringement as established, recommends reviewing both submitted data and generated content, and warns about copyright, trade secrets, design rights, trademarks and passing off.
qs: Consequently, barristers and legal practitioners must critically evaluate both the data provided to LLMs and the content generated by them to ensure compliance with intellectual property and confidentiality laws.
Further, one should be careful not to use, in response to system prompts, words which may breach trademarks or give rise to a passing-off claim.

kp.k: Authoritative research resources support responsible practice
kp.d: The document reports Dame Victoria Sharp's observation that barristers can access authoritative resources through Inn of Court libraries. It identifies research training at qualifying-session, pupillage and continuing professional development stages, in person and remotely, together with document supply services. These are existing supports for competent research, not a proposed AI-specific training curriculum.
qs: The four libraries provide a comprehensive range of legal research resources and training in how to carry out legal research effectively.
They also provide document supply services, to ensure that all members of the Bar have access to authoritative legal resources.

kp.d: The Bar Council advises monitoring Civil Procedure Rules for possible future AI-specific rules or practice directions, including disclosure of AI use in preparing materials. It reports an existing disclosure approach in Manitoba and a Civil Justice Council working group considering rules for AI in civil proceedings; it does not present the possible English requirements as already adopted.
qs: Barristers should also keep abreast of relevant Civil Procedure Rules, which in the future may implement rules/practice directions on the use of LLMs; for example, requiring parties to disclose to the court when they have used generative AI in the preparation of materials.

kp.k: Professional expectations are distinguished from binding regulatory guidance
kp.d: Although framed as reflecting current professional expectations and recent High Court judgments, the document expressly disclaims guidance status under BSB Handbook I6.4. Its recommendations therefore need to be distinguished from the professional duties and judicial findings it discusses.
qs: It is not "guidance" for the purposes of the BSB Handbook I6.4, and neither the BSB nor bodies regulating information security, nor the Legal Ombudsman is bound by any views or advice expressed in it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Bar Council anticipates increasing AI adoption for efficiency and augmentation, alongside continuing human responsibility and substantial professional risks.
pts.d: The Bar Council states that legal professionals increasingly use generative AI for efficiency and practice management and predicts that technological progress and competitive pressures may increase adoption. It suggests that practitioners who understand the tools and use them appropriately will be best placed, rather than predicting replacement of barristers. It presents general-purpose LLMs as unreliable for source-based research and says specialised legal tools also produce hallucinations, requiring independent verification of citations and propositions. AI does not transfer responsibility away from the practitioner. Careless use can expose barristers to sanctions, negligence claims and other liabilities. Further claimed risks include bias, disclosure of confidential or privileged information, data protection and IP infringements, and new cybersecurity attack vectors. The Council also anticipates possible future procedural requirements to disclose AI use in preparing court materials.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The risk claims draw on a legal-research-tool study, court cases and professional duties; the adoption and competitive-position predictions are not quantified.
pts.d: The Bar Council cites the May 2024 Stanford study by Magesh and colleagues, reporting hallucinations on 17%–33% of queries across named Lexis+ AI and Thomson Reuters tools. This is a measured tool-performance claim, distinct from the court incidents cited to illustrate professional consequences. It describes Ayinde as involving five fabricated citations and a misrepresented statutory provision, expressly noting that the lawyers denied using AI; it therefore supplies evidence of consequences for fabricated authorities and inadequate checking, not proof that AI caused that incident. Mata v. Avianca illustrates fabricated ChatGPT authorities and the failure of asking the same system to confirm them. The Council also relies on subsequent Ayinde proceedings, another tribunal case, professional rules, data-protection actions, and IP litigation. Its possible procedural-disclosure prediction is supported by a Manitoba precedent and a Civil Justice Council working group. Its efficiency, adoption and competitive-advantage claims have no quantified productivity, adoption or market evidence in the document. The document expressly disclaims binding BSB guidance status and legal-advice status.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The November 2025 assessment treats present capabilities as unsettled and future adoption and procedural changes as conditional.
pts.d: Issued in January 2024 and last reviewed on 25 November 2025, the document addresses current practice while emphasising rapid technological and regulatory change. The cited hallucination study dates to May 2024, and the principal UK professional-conduct cases to 2025; the reported study range is not presented with a new November 2025 test. Future adoption is qualified by 'may', and the recommendation to use AI by 'if appropriate'. No deadline or magnitude is supplied for adoption growth or possible Civil Procedure Rules changes. Acceptable augmentation depends on understanding the tool, maintaining control, checking outputs and complying with professional and legal obligations. Specialised legal tools may reduce hallucinations but do not reduce the practitioner's responsibility. Confidentiality risks depend in part on how a particular system uses inputs and on protective settings. The Council says only certain legal-practice AI uses trigger the EU AI Act's high-risk obligations and describes the future UK regulatory position as difficult to predict.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Barristers and chambers are the principal audience; clients, courts, legal-service leaders and the public bear related consequences.
pts.d: The document applies to all barristers and chambers in England and Wales. Individual barristers may gain efficiency but retain the work of independent research, verification, analysis and judgment and face disciplinary, civil and reputational consequences for misuse. Chambers must address cybersecurity and, drawing on judicial authority, the Council highlights leadership responsibilities to ensure practitioners understand their obligations. Clients face inaccurate advice and risks to personal data, confidentiality and privilege. Courts face misleading submissions, and the wider justice system faces threats to integrity and public confidence. The cited cases also demonstrate exposure for instructing solicitors. The source does not forecast staffing reductions, fee changes, market-share shifts or access-to-justice gains.
